metadata.title: The Beveridge Curve (Labor Market Slack vs. Openings)
metadata.section: Section B: Macroeconomics, Money & Financial Conditions
metadata.visual_form: Animated Hyperbolic Scatterplot with dynamic regression fits

events.label: Fed rate above 5% to cool the job market

explanation.summary: The Beveridge curve compares how many jobs are open with how many people are unemployed. When employers are desperate for workers, openings are high and unemployment is low. In a recession, it is the other way around.
explanation.methodology: Job openings rate from the BLS Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS, JTS000000000000000JOR). Unemployment rate from BLS (LNS14000000). Federal funds rate from the Federal Reserve via FRED (FEDFUNDS).

key_findings.title: October 2009: Few Jobs, Many Job Seekers
key_findings.description: Unemployment reached 10.0% while the job openings rate was only 1.8%.
key_findings.significance: There were about six unemployed people for each open job.

key_findings.title: March 2022: The Great Labor Shortage
key_findings.description: The job openings rate hit 7.5%, the highest on record, while unemployment was 3.7%. There were about two open jobs for each unemployed person.
key_findings.significance: Employers competed hard for workers, which pushed up wages.

key_findings.title: 2023-2024: Cooling Without a Crash
key_findings.description: The Fed raised its rate from 0.2% to 5.3%. Openings fell to 4.5% while unemployment rose only to 4.1%. As of August 2026, openings are 4.3%.
key_findings.significance: Openings fell a lot before unemployment rose much.
